description: The United States economy in 1949 as seven industries: what each produces, what it buys from the others, and where its output goes. Aggregated to the game's seven sectors and reconciled so that the 1949 national accounts close exactly. A first estimate: to be replaced by an aggregation of the 1947 benchmark input–output table.

sources.label: BLS / BEA 1947 benchmark input–output study (structure of inter-industry flows)
BEA, GDP by industry, historical series (value-added shares)
BEA, Fixed Assets accounts (capital stocks by industry)
Historical Statistics of the United States (foreign trade by commodity)

valueAddedShare.note: Share of business value added, 1949. Farm income fell in 1949; agriculture was about 7% of GDP.

valueAddedRatio.note: Value added per dollar of farm output; the rest is feed, seed, fertiliser, fuel and services.

inputs.note: Where farms' purchased inputs come from: feed grain and livestock from other farms, processed feed, fertiliser and pesticides (technology), fuel, rent and credit, and haulage.

imports.note: Imports of farm products, 1949, $bn: coffee, cocoa, bananas, wool, natural rubber and sugar cane.

capitalShare.note: Share of private fixed capital: farm buildings, tractors and machinery.

investmentShare.note: Share of 1949 private fixed investment, mostly tractors and farm machinery.

valueAddedShare.note: Share of business value added: mining (except oil and gas), metals, fabricated metals, machinery, other transport equipment and construction, together about 15% of 1949 GDP.

valueAddedRatio.note: Heavy industry buys much of its input from itself: ore for steel, steel for machinery, metals and cement for construction.

inputs.note: Mostly its own products, plus lumber (consumer goods), fuel and power, chemicals and electrical parts, rail freight and services.

imports.note: Imports of metals and ores, 1949, $bn: tin, copper, bauxite, manganese, chrome and iron ore.

capitalShare.note: Share of private fixed capital: mines, steel mills, machine shops and contractors' equipment.

valueAddedShare.note: Share of business value added: crude oil and gas, refining, and electric and gas utilities, about 4.3% of 1949 GDP.

valueAddedRatio.note: Refineries buy crude and power stations buy coal, so value added per dollar is modest.

inputs.note: Crude oil to refineries (energy), coal to power stations and pipe and drilling rigs (heavy industry), transport by pipeline, rail and tanker, chemicals, and services.

imports.note: Imports of crude oil and fuel oil, 1949, $bn. The United States was still close to self-sufficient in oil.

capitalShare.note: Share of private fixed capital: power stations, refineries, oil wells and gas mains.

investmentShare.note: Share of 1949 private fixed investment; utility construction boomed after the war.

valueAddedShare.note: Share of business value added: food, textiles, clothing, lumber, furniture, paper, printing, rubber, leather and motor vehicles, about 15% of 1949 GDP.

valueAddedRatio.note: Food processing and car assembly buy most of their value in materials, so value added per dollar is low.

inputs.note: Farm produce for food and cloth, steel for cars and appliances, its own intermediate goods (cloth for clothing, pulp for paper), chemicals and rubber, and freight.

imports.note: Imports of processed consumer goods, 1949, $bn: refined sugar, newsprint, whisky, textiles and finished manufactures.

capitalShare.note: Share of private fixed capital: factories and mills.

investmentShare.note: Share of 1949 private fixed investment, including retooling of car plants.

valueAddedShare.note: Share of business value added: chemicals, electrical machinery, aircraft, instruments and telephone communications, about 6% of 1949 GDP.

valueAddedRatio.note: Value added per dollar of output.

inputs.note: Mostly its own products (chemicals into chemicals, components into equipment), metals, petroleum feedstock, services and freight.

capitalShare.note: Share of private fixed capital: chemical plants, electrical works and the telephone network.

valueAddedShare.note: Share of business value added: finance, insurance, real estate (including housing) and private services, about 19% of 1949 GDP plus the small remainder of industries not listed elsewhere. Government's own workforce is counted separately.

valueAddedRatio.note: Mostly labour and the rental value of housing, so value added per dollar is high.

inputs.note: Building repairs, fuel and power, food and supplies for restaurants and hospitals, telephone service, other services and freight.

imports.note: Imports of services, 1949, $bn: travel abroad and insurance.

capitalShare.note: Share of private fixed capital. Housing alone was almost half of the nation's private fixed capital.

investmentShare.note: Share of 1949 private fixed investment: housebuilding (about a quarter) plus offices and hospitals.

valueAddedShare.note: Share of business value added: transport (about 5.5% of GDP) and wholesale and retail trade (about 17%).

valueAddedRatio.note: Value added per dollar of margin or freight revenue.

inputs.note: Fuel, packaging, paper and tyres, vehicle and railway repairs, rent, advertising and finance, and other carriers' services.

imports.note: Freight carried by foreign ships and airlines, 1949, $bn.

capitalShare.note: Share of private fixed capital: railways (still the largest single item), trucks, ships and shops.

investmentShare.note: Share of 1949 private fixed investment: railway dieselisation, trucks and new stores.

capitalOutputRatio.note: Private fixed capital (including housing) divided by GDP, 1949, in 1949 dollars. BEA fixed-assets figures put the net stock near $475bn.

depreciation.note: Private capital consumption divided by the capital stock, 1949 (about $19bn of $475bn). Each sector's rate is derived so the 1949 accounts balance.

fixed_investment.note: What private fixed investment buys: construction and machinery (heavy industry, about half of it structures), trucks and cars (consumer goods), electrical equipment (technology), brokers' and architects' fees, and dealers' margins.

inventory_investment.note: Which products are stocked or run down: farm stocks, metals, fuel, consumer goods and goods held by merchants.

state_local.note: State and local government spending: half is pay for teachers, police and officials; the rest buys roads and schools (heavy industry), supplies and services.

exports.note: Commercial exports (not aid-financed): grain, cotton and tobacco, machinery, vehicles and steel, coal, consumer manufactures, chemicals, and shipping and financial services.

aid_exports.note: What Marshall Plan dollars bought in America: food, feed and fertiliser, fuel, raw materials and machinery.

defence.note: Defence spending, 1949: about 40% pays servicemen and civilian staff; the rest buys aircraft, electronics and atomic work (technology), ships, tanks, munitions and bases (heavy industry), food and clothing, fuel and transport.

general_government.note: Running the federal government: staff pay, farm price-support purchases (agriculture), supplies and services.

infrastructure.note: Public works: mostly construction and heavy equipment, plus engineers, power and haulage.

research.note: Federal research: government scientists, contracts with laboratories and universities, and equipment.

education_health.note: Federal education and health spending: staff, hospital and school building, medical supplies and services.

physicalIndicators.note: Steel tonnage moves with heavy industry's real output.
